lessons.body:
Part III comes with three PDFs. This lesson tells you what is in each one and how to use it alongside the six topic lessons that follow.

- **Lecture notes** (*Probability and Statistics: Lecture Notes for Data Science*). The full text of the four source lessons, with definitions, derivations, worked examples and 16 exercises with solutions. Read the matching section before or after each topic lesson to see the complete derivations.
- **Lecture slides** (*Introduction to Probability and Statistics*). The 38-slide deck used in class. Look through the slides for a topic before class, then use the topic lesson for step-by-step worked examples you can try yourself.
- **Practice questions** (*Probability and Statistics: 50 multiple-choice questions*). Fifty questions graded Easy, Medium and Hard, with an answer key and worked solutions. In this course the same fifty questions appear in the topic quizzes, so you can try them with your confidence rating and get feedback on the misconception behind a wrong answer.

> [!ghi-nho] The PDFs group the material into four lessons (probability and Bayes' rule; random variables and distributions; joint and sampling distributions; estimation). This course splits it into six topics, so the table below tells you which section of the notes each topic lesson draws on.

| Topic | Lecture notes section |
|---|---|
| 10 Probability foundations | 1 Probability, conditioning and Bayes' rule |
| 11 Random variables and distributions | 2.1–2.7 and 3.6 (functions of random variables) |
| 12 Expectation, variance and moments | 2.8–2.10 |
| 13 Joint distributions and dependence | 3.1–3.5 |
| 14 Sampling distributions and the CLT | 3.7–3.8 |
| 15 Estimation and confidence intervals | 4 Estimation and methods of estimation |

**How to use them.** Skim the slides, work through the topic lesson with pen and paper, take the topic quiz, and only then read the lecture notes for the derivations you want to see in full. Try the exercises at the end of the notes after you finish a topic, and check them against the solutions.

lessons.title: Topic 10 · Probability Foundations
lessons.description: Sample spaces and events, the probability rules, conditioning, independence versus mutual exclusivity, total probability and Bayes' rule.
objectives: Write events from a sample space as sets and combine them with union, intersection and complement
Apply the complement and addition rules to compute probabilities
Compute a conditional probability and build a joint probability with the multiplication rule
Distinguish independent events from mutually exclusive events using their definitions
Use the law of total probability and Bayes' rule to reverse a conditional probability, and explain why the base rate matters
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson you can:
lessons.body:
A spam filter catches 95% of spam. One message gets flagged. How likely is it to be spam? Most people answer "95%", and most people are wrong: the answer also depends on how much of your mail is spam in the first place. This lesson builds the tools that answer questions like this one: events and probabilities, conditioning, independence, and Bayes' rule. The same machinery sits under Naive Bayes classifiers, A/B tests and every probabilistic model you will meet later.

> [!ghi-nho] Probability asks: given a model, which data might we see? Statistics asks the reverse: given the data, what can we say about the model? Bayes' rule at the end of this lesson is the bridge between the two directions.

**Predict first.** A disease affects 1% of a population. A test is positive for 90% of people who have the disease and negative for 90% of people who do not. A randomly chosen person tests positive. Write down your guess for the probability that this person has the disease, then open the box.

:::Check your prediction
The answer is $1/12\approx 0.083$, about 8%. If you guessed something near 90%, you are in good company; the worked example below shows where the intuition goes wrong. Out of 10,000 people, only 90 sick people test positive, while 990 healthy people also test positive.
:::

sections.title: Sample spaces and events

parts.md:
The set $S$ of all possible outcomes of an experiment.

One die roll: $S=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$. Two coin tosses: $S=\{TT, HT, TH, HH\}$.
parts.title: Sample space

parts.md:
A subset of $S$. It occurs exactly when the observed outcome belongs to it.

"Exactly one head" in two tosses is the event $\{HT, TH\}$: a set of outcomes, not the number 1.
parts.title: Event

parts.md:
Let $A=\{2,4,6\}$ (even) and $B=\{4,5,6\}$ (at least four).

$A\cup B=\{2,4,5,6\}$ (at least one occurs), $A\cap B=\{4,6\}$ (both occur), $A^c=\{1,3,5\}$ ($A$ does not occur).
parts.title: Combining events

parts.md:
A probability satisfies $P(A)\ge 0$, $P(S)=1$ and, for disjoint events, $P(\bigcup_i A_i)=\sum_i P(A_i)$.

Consequences: $P(A^c)=1-P(A)$ and $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$.
parts.title: Assigning probability

sections.intro: Everything in probability starts by saying what can happen and which collections of outcomes we care about.
sections.outro: > [!canh-bao] Counting favourable outcomes over total outcomes, $P(A)=|A|/|S|$, is valid only when the outcomes are equally likely. “Rain” and “no rain” are two outcomes, but not a 50/50 split.

sections.title: Worked example: an even result or a result of at least four

parts.md:
$$S=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\},\quad A=\{2,4,6\},\quad B=\{4,5,6\}$$

Why: probabilities attach to events, so write the events as sets first.
parts.title: List the sets

parts.md:
$$P(A)=\tfrac36,\qquad P(B)=\tfrac36,\qquad P(A\cap B)=P(\{4,6\})=\tfrac26$$

Why: a balanced die makes the six outcomes equally likely, so each probability is a count divided by 6.
parts.title: Probability of each piece

parts.md:
$$P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)=\tfrac36+\tfrac36-\tfrac26=\tfrac46=\tfrac23$$

Why: the outcomes 4 and 6 sit in both $A$ and $B$, so they are counted twice in $P(A)+P(B)$ and must be subtracted once.
parts.title: Addition rule

parts.md:
$$A\cup B=\{2,4,5,6\}\;\Rightarrow\;P(A\cup B)=\tfrac46\;✓$$

Why: whenever you can list the outcomes, counting gives an independent check of the rule.
parts.title: Check by counting

parts.md:
$$P(A^c)=1-P(A)=1-\tfrac12=\tfrac12$$

Why: $A$ and $A^c$ partition $S$, so their probabilities add to 1.
parts.title: Complement

sections.intro: A balanced die is rolled once, with $A=\{2,4,6\}$ and $B=\{4,5,6\}$. Find $P(A\cup B)$ and $P(A^c)$. Try each step yourself before pressing Next.

sections.title: Independent versus mutually exclusive

parts.md:
Learning that $B$ occurred does not change the probability of $A$.

$$P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B)\iff P(A\mid B)=P(A)\quad(P(B)>0)$$

It is a statement about **probabilities**.

Example: two fair coins, $A$ = first is heads, $B$ = second is heads. $P(A\cap B)=\tfrac14=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12$.
parts.title: Independent events

parts.md:
The events cannot occur together.

$$A\cap B=\varnothing\quad\Rightarrow\quad P(A\cap B)=0$$

It is a statement about **which outcomes they share**.

Example: one die roll, $A=\{1,2\}$ and $B=\{5,6\}$. If $A$ occurs, $B$ certainly did not.
parts.title: Mutually exclusive (disjoint) events

sections.outro: > [!canh-bao] If $P(A)>0$ and $P(B)>0$ and the events are disjoint, they are never independent: $P(A\cap B)=0$ but $P(A)P(B)>0$. The die events $A$ and $B$ above are neither disjoint nor independent, since $P(A\cap B)=\tfrac13$ while $P(A)P(B)=\tfrac14$.

sections.title: Worked example: conditioning and the multiplication rule

parts.md:
Given $B=\{4,5,6\}$, three equally likely outcomes remain, and two of them are even:

$$P(A\mid B)=\tfrac23$$

Why: learning that $B$ occurred throws away every outcome outside $B$.
parts.title: Restrict attention to the conditioning event

parts.md:
$$P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}=\frac{2/6}{3/6}=\frac23$$

Why: the numerator is the probability shared by the two events; the denominator rescales $P(B)$ to 1.
parts.title: Get the same answer from the formula

parts.md:
$$P(A\cap B)=P(A\mid B)\,P(B)$$

Why: this is how you build a joint probability from a conditional one, which is how models are usually specified.
parts.title: Rearrange to the multiplication rule

parts.md:
$$P(S\cap F)=P(F\mid S)\,P(S)=0.60\times0.20=0.12$$

So 12% of all messages are spam that contain “free”.
parts.title: Use it in the spam model

parts.md:
$P(F\mid S)=0.60$ is the share of spam that contains “free”. The question “What share of messages containing ‘free’ is spam?” is $P(S\mid F)$, a different number (computed in the next example).

In the die example $P(A\mid B)=P(B\mid A)=\tfrac23$ only because $P(A)=P(B)$.
parts.title: Do not flip the conditional

sections.intro: First the die, then a spam filter. In the spam model, 20% of messages are spam ($S$), 60% of spam contains the word “free” ($F$), and 5% of non-spam contains it.

sections.title: Worked example: total probability and Bayes' rule for spam

parts.md:
$S$ and $S^c$ split every message into two disjoint groups that together cover everything:

$$P(S)=0.20,\quad P(S^c)=0.80,\quad P(F\mid S)=0.60,\quad P(F\mid S^c)=0.05$$
parts.title: Name the partition and list the givens

parts.md:
$$P(F)=P(F\mid S)P(S)+P(F\mid S^c)P(S^c)=0.60(0.20)+0.05(0.80)=0.12+0.04=0.16$$

Why: a message with “free” arrives through exactly one branch, spam or non-spam, so add the two weighted branches.
parts.title: Law of total probability

parts.md:
$$P(S\mid F)=\frac{P(F\mid S)P(S)}{P(F)}=\frac{0.12}{0.16}=0.75$$

Why: the numerator is the spam-with-“free” branch; the denominator is all messages with “free”.
parts.title: Bayes' rule

parts.md:
Take 10,000 messages. 2,000 are spam, and 1,200 of those contain “free”. 8,000 are not spam, and 400 of those contain “free”.

$$\frac{1200}{1200+400}=0.75\;✓$$
parts.title: Check with counts

parts.md:
If only 2% of messages are spam, with the same likelihoods:

$$P(F)=0.60(0.02)+0.05(0.98)=0.061,\qquad P(S\mid F)=\frac{0.012}{0.061}\approx0.197$$

Why: the evidence did not change, the prior did. Bayes' rule always uses both.
parts.title: Change the base rate

sections.intro: Use the spam model above: $P(S)=0.20$, $P(F\mid S)=0.60$, $P(F\mid S^c)=0.05$. What is $P(S\mid F)$?

sections.title: Worked example: a positive diagnostic result

parts.title: Total probability of a positive result

parts.md:
| | Positive | Negative | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Disease | 90 | 10 | 100 |
| No disease | 990 | 8,910 | 9,900 |
| Total | 1,080 | 8,920 | 10,000 |

Why: only 90 of the 1,080 positive results come from people who are sick. The 8.3% is a share of the positive column, not the 90% sensitivity.
parts.title: Read it as expected counts

sections.intro: The prediction problem from the start: $P(D)=0.01$, $P(+\mid D)=0.90$ and $P(+\mid D^c)=0.10$ (the false-positive rate, which is 1 minus the specificity). Find $P(D\mid +)$.
sections.outro: > [!meo] When Bayes' rule feels abstract, imagine 10,000 people and count. Rows carry the base rate, columns carry the likelihoods, and the answer is one cell divided by a column total.

sections.title: The diagnostic example at a glance

parts.md: of the population has the disease: the **base rate** $P(D)$.
of sick people test positive: the **sensitivity** $P(+\mid D)$.
of positive tests belong to a sick person: the answer $P(D\mid +)=1/12$.

sections.outro: > [!ghi-nho] The first two numbers are inputs; the third is the output. Confusing the second with the third is the most common mistake in conditional probability.

sections.title: Find the error in the solution

parts.md:
Two students each wrote a solution. Find the mistake in each **before** opening the answer.

**Solution 1** (spam model: $P(S)=0.2$, $P(F\mid S)=0.6$, $P(F\mid S^c)=0.05$).

> **Step 1.** The given probabilities are $P(S)=0.2$, $P(F\mid S)=0.6$ and $P(F\mid S^c)=0.05$.

> **Step 2.** By Bayes' rule, $P(S\mid F)=P(F\mid S)\,P(S)=0.6\times0.2=0.12$.

> **Step 3.** So a message containing “free” is spam with probability 12%.

:::Where is the error in Solution 1?
Step 2 leaves out the denominator. $0.12$ is the joint probability $P(S\cap F)$. Bayes' rule divides by $P(F)=0.16$, giving $P(S\mid F)=0.75$. A sanity check would have caught it: seeing “free” is evidence *for* spam, so the probability of spam should rise above the 20% base rate, not fall to 12%.
:::

**Solution 2.** Events $A$ and $B$ have $P(A)=0.5$ and $P(B)=0.3$ and cannot occur together. “So they are independent, and $P(A\cup B)=0.5+0.3-0.5\cdot0.3=0.65$.”

:::Where is the error in Solution 2?
Events that cannot occur together are *mutually exclusive*, not independent. Because $P(A)P(B)=0.15\neq0=P(A\cap B)$, they are dependent. Since the overlap is empty, $P(A\cup B)=0.5+0.3=0.8$.
:::

sections.title: Common questions

parts.md: The 90% is $P(+\mid D)$, conditioned on the sick people. The question asks for $P(D\mid +)$, conditioned on everyone who tested positive. These have different denominators, and the second one depends on how common the disease is.
parts.title: Why can't I just use the test's 90% accuracy?

parts.md: Yes, when $P(A)=P(B)$ and the overlap is positive, because $P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)$ and $P(B\mid A)=P(A\cap B)/P(A)$. That is a coincidence of the numbers, not a rule.
parts.title: Can P(A | B) ever equal P(B | A)?

parts.md: Then $P(A\mid B)$ is not defined by the formula, because it would divide by zero. You cannot condition on an event that has probability zero in this framework.
parts.title: What if P(B) = 0?

parts.md: Yes. $P(A\cap B^c)=P(A)-P(A\cap B)=P(A)-P(A)P(B)=P(A)\,(1-P(B))=P(A)P(B^c)$.
parts.title: If A and B are independent, are A and B^c independent too?

parts.md: No. They must be pairwise disjoint, cover the whole sample space, and each have positive probability. Their probabilities then act as the weights in the law of total probability.
parts.title: Must the events in a partition be equally likely?

sections.title: Practice with Python

parts.md:
Sets make events concrete, and a simulation lets you check Bayes' rule without any algebra. The first snippet uses exact fractions; the second simulates one million people with a fixed random seed. ```html 
from fractions import Fraction as F

S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}
A = {2, 4, 6}          # even
B = {4, 5, 6}          # at least four
P = lambda E: F(len(E), len(S))   # equally likely outcomes

print("A | B  =", sorted(A | B), " P =", P(A | B))
print("A & B  =", sorted(A & B), " P =", P(A & B))
print("A^c    =", sorted(S - A), " P =", P(S - A))
print("P(A|B) =", P(A & B) / P(B))
print("independent?", P(A & B) == P(A) * P(B))

Output

A | B  = [2, 4, 5, 6]  P = 2/3
A & B  = [4, 6]  P = 1/3
A^c    = [1, 3, 5]  P = 1/2
P(A|B) = 2/3
independent? False
``` The simulated posterior is close to the exact $1/12$ (about 0.0833), with a small gap that shrinks as the simulation grows. ```html 
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n = 1_000_000
disease = rng.random(n) < 0.01                       # base rate 1%
positive = np.where(disease, rng.random(n) < 0.90,   # sensitivity 0.90
                              rng.random(n) < 0.10)  # false-positive rate 0.10

print("P(positive)      ~", round(positive.mean(), 4))
print("P(disease | pos) ~", round(disease[positive].mean(), 4))
print("Bayes (exact)    =", round(0.90 * 0.01 / (0.90 * 0.01 + 0.10 * 0.99), 4))

Output

P(positive)      ~ 0.1081
P(disease | pos) ~ 0.0832
Bayes (exact)    = 0.0833
```

items.meaning: The set S of all possible outcomes of an experiment.
A subset of the sample space; it occurs when the outcome belongs to it.
items.example: Exactly one head in two tosses is {HT, TH}.

items.meaning: Aᶜ = S \ A, the event that A does not occur; P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A).
P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).
P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B), defined when P(B) > 0.
P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B), equivalently P(A | B) = P(A).
items.example: Two fair coins: first heads and second heads.

items.meaning: A ∩ B is empty. With positive probabilities they are never independent.
P(A) = Σ P(A | Bi)P(Bi) over a partition B1, …, Bk.
P(Bj | A) = P(A | Bj)P(Bj) / Σ P(A | Bi)P(Bi): it reverses a conditional using the base rates.
items.example: 1% prevalence, 90% sensitivity, 10% false positives give P(D | +) = 1/12.

summary: An event is a set of outcomes; its probability obeys the addition rule, which subtracts the overlap, and the complement rule.
Conditioning on B restricts attention to B: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B), and P(A | B) is generally different from P(B | A).
Independent means P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B); mutually exclusive means A ∩ B is empty. With positive probabilities, disjoint events are never independent.
The law of total probability weights each branch of a partition by its probability; Bayes' rule divides one weighted branch by that total.
A rare event stays rare after a positive signal unless the signal is very strong, so always ask for the base rate before trusting a likelihood.

questions.prompt: Two coins are tossed, with sample space $S=\{TT, HT, TH, HH\}$. Which event represents exactly one head?
questions.explanation: Exactly one head occurs for $HT$ and $TH$, so the event is $\{HT, TH\}$. An event is a set of outcomes; $\{0,1,2\}$ lists values of the head count, which is a random variable, not outcomes of the experiment.

questions.prompt: If $P(A)=0.40$, $P(B)=0.50$ and $P(A\cap B)=0.20$, what is $P(A\cup B)$?
questions.explanation: The addition rule gives $P(A\cup B)=0.40+0.50-0.20=0.70$. The intersection is subtracted because its outcomes are counted in both $P(A)$ and $P(B)$. Plain addition (0.90) counts them twice.

questions.prompt: If $P(A\cap B)=0.12$ and $P(B)=0.30$, what is $P(A\mid B)$?
questions.explanation: Conditioning gives $P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)=0.12/0.30=0.40$. Option 0.12 is the joint probability with no division, and 0.036 multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.prompt: Events $A$ and $B$ are disjoint, and both have positive probability. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: Disjointness gives $P(A\cap B)=0$, but $P(A)P(B)>0$. The equality required for independence therefore fails. Equivalently, $P(A\mid B)=0\neq P(A)$.

questions.prompt: Events $B_1, B_2$ partition the sample space. If $P(B_1)=0.60$, $P(B_2)=0.40$, $P(A\mid B_1)=0.10$ and $P(A\mid B_2)=0.30$, what is $P(A)$?
questions.explanation: Total probability gives $P(A)=0.10(0.60)+0.30(0.40)=0.06+0.12=0.18$. The conditional probabilities must be weighted by the partition probabilities: the sum 0.40 and the plain average 0.20 ignore the weights, and 0.06 keeps only one branch.

questions.prompt: In a hypothetical detection model, 2% of records are anomalous. A detector flags 90% of anomalies and 10% of non-anomalies. Given a flag, what is the probability of an anomaly, approximately?
questions.explanation: Let $D$ be anomaly and $F$ be flag. Bayes' rule gives $P(D\mid F)=\dfrac{0.90(0.02)}{0.90(0.02)+0.10(0.98)}=\dfrac{0.018}{0.116}=\dfrac9{58}\approx0.1552$. The 0.90 is $P(F\mid D)$, the numerator alone is 0.018, and the denominator alone is 0.116.

questions.prompt: Events $A$ and $B$ are independent, with $P(A)=0.40$ and $P(B)=0.50$. What is $P(A^c\cap B)$?
questions.explanation: Independence gives $P(A\cap B)=0.40(0.50)=0.20$. Subtract this part from $P(B)$: $P(A^c\cap B)=0.50-0.20=0.30$. Equivalently $P(A^c)P(B)=0.60(0.50)=0.30$.

questions.prompt: In a hypothetical model, $P(D)=0.01$. Two detectors each flag with probability 0.90 given $D$ and 0.10 given $D^c$. Their flags are independent conditional on either state. If both flag, what is $P(D\mid \text{both flags})$?
questions.explanation: Conditional independence gives $0.90^2=0.81$ and $0.10^2=0.01$ for two flags in the two states. Bayes' rule gives $\dfrac{0.81(0.01)}{0.81(0.01)+0.01(0.99)}=\dfrac{0.0081}{0.018}=0.45$. One flag alone would give only $1/12$; the 0.81 and 0.90 are likelihoods, not posteriors.

questions.prompt: Events $A$ and $B$ are independent with $P(A)=0.5$ and $P(B)=0.3$. Find $P(A\cup B)$ as a decimal.
questions.explanation: Independence gives $P(A\cap B)=0.5\times0.3=0.15$. The addition rule then gives $P(A\cup B)=0.5+0.3-0.15=0.65$.

questions.prompt: Two events that each have positive probability and cannot occur together can still be independent.
questions.explanation: False. If $A\cap B=\varnothing$ then $P(A\cap B)=0$, while independence would require $P(A)P(B)>0$. Disjoint events with positive probability are always dependent.

questions.prompt: A fraud detector is applied to transactions of which 1% are fraudulent. It flags 80% of fraudulent transactions and 5% of legitimate ones. Given that a transaction is flagged, what is the probability that it is fraudulent? Give a decimal to 3 places.
questions.explanation: $P(\text{flag})=0.80(0.01)+0.05(0.99)=0.008+0.0495=0.0575$, so $P(\text{fraud}\mid\text{flag})=\dfrac{0.008}{0.0575}=\dfrac{16}{115}\approx0.139$. Most flagged transactions are legitimate because legitimate ones are 99 times more common.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of a Bayes' rule calculation in a sensible order.
questions.explanation: Name the events and givens first. The denominator comes from total probability, the numerator from the multiplication rule, and the division gives the posterior. A count table is a quick independent check.
sequence: Define the events and write down the given probabilities
Compute the evidence probability with the law of total probability
Compute the numerator P(evidence | hypothesis) × P(hypothesis)
Divide the numerator by the evidence probability
Check the answer with expected counts out of 10,000

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
questions.explanation: The sample space is the whole set of outcomes and an event is a subset of it. The complement is everything outside $A$. Disjointness is about shared outcomes, independence is about the product rule for probabilities.

pairs.right: The set of all possible outcomes
A subset of the sample space
The event that A does not occur

lessons.title: Topic 11 · Random Variables and Distributions
lessons.description: Random variables, mass functions and densities, the CDF, and the Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson, uniform, exponential and normal distributions.
objectives: Explain a random variable as a function and write events such as {X = 1} in terms of outcomes
Distinguish a mass function from a density and compute probabilities from each
Build and read a CDF, and use it to compute P(a < X ≤ b)
Choose among the Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson, uniform, exponential and normal models for a described situation
Standardize a normal variable and compute normal probabilities
Find the density of a linear transformation of a continuous random variable
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson you can:
lessons.body:
Data arrive as numbers: a click indicator, the number of requests per minute, a sensor reading, the time until a server fails. A **random variable** is the bridge that turns the outcome of an uncertain experiment into such a number, and its **distribution** says how the probability is spread across the possible values. Choosing the right distribution is the first modelling decision in almost every statistical or machine learning method: Bernoulli for a yes/no label, Poisson for event counts, Normal for noise.

> [!ghi-nho] A discrete variable has a **probability mass function** whose heights are probabilities. A continuous variable has a **density** whose heights are *not* probabilities; probabilities are the areas under it. The **cumulative distribution function** (CDF) $F_X(x)=P(X\le x)$ works for both.

**Predict first.** A continuous variable has the density $f(x)=2$ on the interval $0\le x\le 0.5$ and $f(x)=0$ elsewhere. Is this a valid density, even though $2$ is larger than $1$? Decide, and then open the box.

:::Check your prediction
Yes, it is valid. The area is the height times the width, $2\times0.5=1$, and probabilities are areas. This is the Uniform distribution on $[0,0.5]$. A density value is not a probability, so values above 1 are allowed.
:::

sections.title: Worked example: a head count on two tosses

parts.md:
$S=\{TT,HT,TH,HH\}$, and $X$ is a function on $S$:

| Outcome $\omega$ | TT | HT | TH | HH |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $X(\omega)$ | 0 | 1 | 1 | 2 |

Why: each outcome receives exactly one number, but two outcomes may receive the same number.
parts.title: The sample space and the function

parts.md:
$\{X=1\}$ is shorthand for the event $\{HT,TH\}$, so $P(X=1)$ is an ordinary event probability.

Why: this ties the new notation back to the sample space and events of Topic 10.
parts.title: Events written with $X$

parts.md:
Fair and independent tosses make each outcome have probability $1/4$:

$$p_X(0)=\tfrac14,\qquad p_X(1)=\tfrac12,\qquad p_X(2)=\tfrac14,\qquad \sum_x p_X(x)=1$$

Why: fairness and independence are modelling assumptions; the definition of a random variable does not require them.
parts.title: Probability mass function

parts.md:
$$F_X(x)=P(X\le x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt0\\ 1/4,&0\le x\lt1\\ 3/4,&1\le x\lt2\\ 1,&x\ge2\end{cases}$$

Why: the CDF accumulates point masses, so it jumps by $1/4$, $1/2$ and $1/4$ at 0, 1 and 2.
parts.title: CDF

parts.md:
$$P(X\le1)=F_X(1)=\tfrac34,\qquad P(X=1)=F_X(1)-F_X(0)=\tfrac34-\tfrac14=\tfrac12$$

Why: the probability of a single value is the *jump* of the CDF there, not the CDF value itself.
parts.title: Read probabilities off the CDF

sections.intro: Two fair coins are tossed independently and $X$ counts heads. Build the random variable, its probability mass function and its CDF, one piece at a time.

sections.title: Probability mass function versus density

parts.md:
Possible values form a finite or countable set.

$$p_X(x)=P(X=x),\qquad p_X(x)\ge0,\qquad \sum_x p_X(x)=1$$

Heights **are** probabilities, so they cannot exceed 1. Probabilities of events add heights. The CDF jumps.
parts.title: Discrete: probability mass function

parts.md:
Probabilities are areas under the curve.

$$P(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^b f_X(x)\,dx,\qquad f_X\ge0,\qquad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_X=1$$

Heights are **not** probabilities and can exceed 1. $P(X=x_0)=0$ for every single point. The CDF is continuous, and its derivative is the density.
parts.title: Continuous: probability density function

sections.outro: > [!canh-bao] A density of height $2$ on an interval of width $0.5$ is fine because the area is $1$. Never read $f_X(x_0)$ as “the probability that $X=x_0$”. For a continuous variable that probability is $0$.

sections.title: Worked example: the CDF of a Bernoulli and of an exponential variable

parts.md:
$$F_X(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt0\\0.80,&0\le x\lt1\\1,&x\ge1\end{cases}$$

Why: the jumps are $0.80$ at $0$ and $0.20$ at $1$.
parts.title: Bernoulli CDF

parts.md:
$$f_X(x)=\tfrac12e^{-x/2}\ (x\gt0),\qquad F_X(x)=\int_0^x\tfrac12e^{-t/2}dt=1-e^{-x/2}\ (x\ge0)$$

Why: the integration variable $t$ is a dummy, and $x$ is the upper endpoint.
parts.title: Exponential density and CDF

parts.md:
$$P(X\gt t)=1-F_X(t)=e^{-t/\beta},\qquad P(X\gt2)=e^{-1}\approx0.3679$$

Why: with $\beta=2$ a waiting time exceeds two time units with probability about 37%. For a continuous variable the endpoints do not matter; for a discrete variable they can.

One yes/no trial. Support $\{0,1\}$.

$P(X=1)=p$, $P(X=0)=1-p$, i.e. $p^x(1-p)^{1-x}$.

Use: a click, a spam label, a pass/fail outcome.

parts.md:
The number of successes in $n$ independent trials with the same $p$.

$$P(K=k)=\binom nk p^k(1-p)^{n-k},\ k=0,\dots,n$$

Use: successes among $n$ website visitors.

A count of events in a fixed exposure (one minute, one page) at a stable rate; support $0,1,2,\dots$

Use: requests per minute, defects per metre.

parts.md:
All values in $[a,b]$ equally likely.

$$f_X(x)=\frac1{b-a},\quad a\le x\le b$$

Use: a random position, a random seed; probability = interval length / $(b-a)$.
parts.title: Uniform(a, b)

parts.md:
A waiting time with **scale** (mean) $\beta$, support $x\gt0$.

$$f_X(x)=\tfrac1\beta e^{-x/\beta},\qquad P(X\gt t)=e^{-t/\beta}$$

Use: time until the next event. $\beta$ is a mean, not a rate.
parts.title: Exponential(β)

parts.md:
A symmetric bell shape with mean $\mu$ and **variance** $\sigma^2$ as its second parameter.

$$f_X(x)=\frac1{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\Big[-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big]$$

Use: measurement noise, and the limit of averages (Topic 14).

parts.md:
Five independent trials with $p=0.20$:

$$P(K=2)=\binom52(0.20)^2(0.80)^3=10(0.04)(0.512)=0.2048$$

Why: $\binom52=10$ counts the sequences with two successes, and each has probability $p^2(1-p)^3$.
parts.title: Binomial: exactly two successes in five trials

parts.md:
$$P(K=0)=0.80^{20}\approx0.0115,\qquad E(K)=np=4,\quad V(K)=np(1-p)=3.2$$

Why: all twenty trials must fail. These are model calculations for a given $p$, not estimates from data.
parts.title: Binomial: no successes in twenty trials

parts.md:
With $\lambda=3$ events expected per exposure:

$$P(X=0)=e^{-3}\approx0.0498\;\Rightarrow\;P(X\ge1)=1-e^{-3}\approx0.9502$$

Why: the complement rule avoids summing an infinite series.

parts.md:
$X\sim N(100,225)$, so $\mu=100$ and $\sigma^2=225$, hence $\sigma=15$.

Why: the second parameter is the variance, so take its square root before standardizing.

parts.md:
$$P(100\le X\le130)=\Phi(2)-\Phi(0)\approx0.9772-0.5=0.4772$$

Why: an interval is a difference of two cumulative probabilities.
parts.title: Use the CDF difference

parts.md:
$X\sim N(10,4)$ has $\sigma=2$, so $8\le X\le12$ becomes $-1\le Z\le1$:

$$2\Phi(1)-1\approx2(0.8413)-1=0.6826$$

Why: the standard normal is symmetric, so $\Phi(-1)=1-\Phi(1)$. With more digits the value is $0.6827$, the familiar 68% within one standard deviation.
parts.title: A second case with symmetry

sections.intro: Convert to the standard normal $Z=(X-\mu)/\sigma$, then use $\Phi$ (given: $\Phi(1)\approx0.8413$ and $\Phi(2)\approx0.9772$).

parts.md:
$$\int_0^1cx\,dx=\frac c2=1\;\Rightarrow\;c=2$$

Why: total area must be 1.
parts.title: Normalise

parts.md: $$F_X(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt0\\x^2,&0\le x\le1\\1,&x\gt1\end{cases}\qquad P(X\gt\tfrac12)=1-\tfrac14=\tfrac34$$
parts.title: CDF of X

parts.md:
As $x$ goes from 0 to 1, $u$ goes from $-1$ to $2$. For $-1\le u\le2$:

$$F_U(u)=P(3X-1\le u)=F_X\!\Big(\frac{u+1}3\Big)=\Big(\frac{u+1}3\Big)^2\;\Rightarrow\;f_U(u)=\frac{2(u+1)}9$$

Why: find the CDF first, then differentiate; the chain rule supplies the factor $1/3$.
parts.title: An increasing map: U = 3X − 1

parts.md:
Now $v$ runs from $1$ down to $-1$. The inequality **reverses**:

$$F_V(v)=P(1-2X\le v)=P\Big(X\ge\frac{1-v}2\Big)=1-\Big(\frac{1-v}2\Big)^2\;\Rightarrow\;f_V(v)=\frac{1-v}2,\ -1\lt v\lt1$$

Why: dividing by the negative number $-2$ flips the inequality, so you must use $1-F_X$.
parts.title: A decreasing map: V = 1 − 2X

parts.md:
$$\int_{-1}^{2}\frac{2(u+1)}9du=1\qquad\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{1-v}2dv=1$$

Why: any valid density integrates to 1 over its support. Always determine the transformed support before writing the final formula.
parts.title: Check the new densities

sections.title: Find the error in the solution

parts.md:
A student answers: “Let $X$ be uniform on $[0,0.5]$. Its density is $f_X(x)=2$. Since a probability cannot exceed 1, $f_X(x)=2$ is impossible, so a uniform variable on $[0,0.5]$ does not exist.”

Another student continues: “Anyway, $P(X=0.3)=f_X(0.3)=2$.”

:::What is wrong with these two statements?
**First statement.** The density is a height, not a probability. The area under it is $2\times0.5=1$, so it is a valid density. Only the *areas* must be at most 1.

**Second statement.** For a continuous variable $P(X=0.3)=0$. The number 2 is the density at 0.3 (probability per unit length), so the probability that $X$ lies in a short interval of width $0.01$ around 0.3 is about $2\times0.01=0.02$.
:::

parts.md: There are uncountably many possible values, so a single value gets area zero. Probability lives on intervals. This is why $P(a\le X\le b)$ and $P(a\lt X\lt b)$ are equal for a continuous variable but can differ for a discrete one.

parts.md:
The `scipy.stats` module has the pmf or density (`pmf`, `pdf`), the CDF (`cdf`), and the tail (`sf`) for every distribution in this lesson. Check the probabilities from the worked examples, and note that a density can exceed 1: ```html 
from scipy import stats

print("Bin(5, 0.2):  P(K=2)      =", round(stats.binom.pmf(2, 5, 0.2), 4))
print("Poisson(3):   P(X=0)      =", round(stats.poisson.pmf(0, 3), 4), "  P(X>=1) =", round(stats.poisson.sf(0, 3), 4))
print("Exp(scale=2): P(1<=X<=3)  =", round(stats.expon.cdf(3, scale=2) - stats.expon.cdf(1, scale=2), 4))
print("N(100, 15^2): P(100<=X<=130) =", round(stats.norm.cdf(130, 100, 15) - stats.norm.cdf(100, 100, 15), 4))
print("N(10, 4):     P(8<=X<=12)    =", round(stats.norm.cdf(12, 10, 2) - stats.norm.cdf(8, 10, 2), 4))
print("Uniform(0, 0.5) density at 0.3 =", stats.uniform.pdf(0.3, loc=0, scale=0.5))

Output

Bin(5, 0.2):  P(K=2)      = 0.2048
Poisson(3):   P(X=0)      = 0.0498   P(X>=1) = 0.9502
Exp(scale=2): P(1<=X<=3)  = 0.3834
N(100, 15^2): P(100<=X<=130) = 0.4772
N(10, 4):     P(8<=X<=12)    = 0.6827
Uniform(0, 0.5) density at 0.3 = 2.0
``` A simulation can also verify a transformed density. Here $X$ has density $2x$ (sampled by taking the square root of a uniform number, because $F_X(x)=x^2$), and we check $U=3X-1$: ```html 
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
x = np.sqrt(rng.random(1_000_000))     # inverse-CDF sampling: F(x) = x^2, so X = sqrt(Uniform)
u = 3 * x - 1                          # U = 3X - 1, density 2(u+1)/9 on (-1, 2)

print("empirical P(0 < U <= 1) =", round(((u > 0) & (u <= 1)).mean(), 4))
print("from the density        =", round(((1 + 1) ** 2 - (0 + 1) ** 2) / 9, 4))
print("mean of U               =", round(u.mean(), 3), " (theory: 3*(2/3) - 1 = 1)")

Output

empirical P(0 < U <= 1) = 0.3334
from the density        = 0.3333
mean of U               = 1.0  (theory: 3*(2/3) - 1 = 1)
```

f(x) ≥ 0 with P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ f over [a, b]; heights are not probabilities and can exceed 1.

summary: A random variable is a function from outcomes to numbers; {X = x} is an event, and its probability is an ordinary event probability.
A mass function gives probabilities at points; a density gives probabilities as areas, and its heights can exceed 1. For a continuous variable, P(X = x) = 0.
The CDF F(x) = P(X ≤ x) describes both kinds of variable, and interval probabilities are differences of the CDF.
Match the situation to the distribution: Bernoulli (one trial), Binomial (count of successes), Poisson (event count), Uniform, Exponential (waiting time), Normal (symmetric noise).
For a normal probability, standardize with the standard deviation, then use Φ(upper) − Φ(lower).
To find the density of g(X), find the CDF first, remember that a decreasing map reverses the inequality, and check that the density integrates to 1.

quiz.title: Check your understanding · Random Variables and Distributions

questions.prompt: Which statement defines a random variable $X:S\to\mathbb R$?
questions.explanation: A random variable is a fixed real-valued function of an uncertain outcome. Different outcomes may have the same numerical value (HT and TH both give a head count of 1), and the values need not be equally likely.

options.label: It assigns a probability to each event.
It assigns one real number to each outcome.
It must have equally likely possible values.
It must take a new value for every outcome.

questions.prompt: Let $X$ have a probability density $f_X$. Which statement always holds for a fixed real number $x_0$?
questions.explanation: For a variable with a density, a single point has zero probability. Probabilities are integrals over sets; a density height may exceed one, and the total area is 1, not 0.

questions.prompt: If $X\sim N(10,4)$, with the second parameter denoting variance, which expression has a standard normal distribution?
questions.explanation: Standardization subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation: $\sigma=\sqrt4=2$, so $Z=(X-10)/2$. Dividing by 4 uses the variance, and $X/2$ or $(X+10)/2$ does not centre at the mean.

questions.prompt: Five independent trials have the same success probability $p=0.20$. What is the probability of exactly two successes?
questions.explanation: The success count is binomial. Thus $P(K=2)=\binom52(0.20)^2(0.80)^3=10(0.04)(0.512)=0.2048$. The value 0.0512 is $P(K=3)$ (exponents swapped), 0.4096 is $P(K=1)$, and 0.20 is just $p$.

questions.prompt: Let $X\sim\text{Uniform}(2,8)$. What is the pair $\big(P(3\lt X\lt5),\,V(X)\big)$?
questions.explanation: The probability is interval length divided by support length: $(5-3)/(8-2)=1/3$. The variance is $(8-2)^2/12=3$.

questions.prompt: Let $X\sim N(100,225)$. Using $\Phi(2)\approx0.9772$, approximate $P(100\le X\le130)$.
questions.explanation: Here $\sigma=15$, so the endpoints standardize to 0 and 2. The probability is $\Phi(2)-\Phi(0)\approx0.9772-0.5=0.4772$. The value 0.9772 forgets to subtract $\Phi(0)$, 0.9544 would be $P(70\le X\le130)$, and 0.0228 is the upper tail.

questions.prompt: Let $f_X(x)=2x$ for $0\lt x\lt1$, and define $U=2-3X$. Which density is correct on $-1\lt u\lt2$, with density zero elsewhere?
questions.explanation: For $-1\lt u\lt2$, $F_U(u)=P(X\ge(2-u)/3)=1-[(2-u)/3]^2$. Differentiation gives $f_U(u)=2(2-u)/9$. The decreasing transformation reverses the inequality; $2(u+1)/9$ is the density for the increasing map $3X-1$, and dropping the factor $1/3$ gives $2(2-u)/3$.

questions.prompt: The number of requests per minute is modelled as Poisson with $\lambda=2$. Find $P(X=0)$ to 4 decimal places.
A continuous random variable can have a density that takes the value 3 at some point.
questions.explanation: True. A density value is not a probability. For example, the density of Uniform(0, 1/3) equals 3 everywhere on $[0,1/3]$ and its total area is $3\times\tfrac13=1$.

questions.prompt: Match each distribution to the situation it models best.
questions.explanation: Bernoulli is a single trial, binomial counts successes over $n$ trials, Poisson counts events over an exposure, exponential models the waiting time, uniform is flat on an interval, and the normal is the symmetric bell shape used for noise and for averages.

lessons.description: Expectation and its linearity, variance and standard deviation, shift and scale rules, the moments of standard distributions, and raw moments.
objectives: Compute the expectation of a discrete or continuous random variable and of a function g(X)
Use linearity of expectation, and state when independence is not required
Compute a variance from the definition and from the shortcut E(X²) − [E(X)]²
Apply the shift and scale rules for the mean and variance of aX + b
Recall the mean and variance of the standard distributions and avoid parameter mix-ups
Compute raw moments and the mean squared distance E[(X − c)²]
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson you can:
lessons.body:
A distribution contains a lot of information, and in practice we summarise it with a few numbers. The **expectation** is the long-run average and tells you where the distribution is centred. The **variance** tells you how far outcomes typically fall from that centre. In machine learning the squared error $E[(Y-c)^2]$ is the quantity a regression model tries to minimise, and the mean and variance of an estimator are exactly what Topic 15 uses to judge it.

> [!ghi-nho] Expectation is a probability-weighted average: $E[g(X)]=\sum_x g(x)\,p_X(x)$ for a discrete variable and $\int g(x)f_X(x)\,dx$ for a continuous one. It is **linear**, $E(aX+bY+c)=aE(X)+bE(Y)+c$, with no independence needed. Variance is **not** linear: $V(aX+b)=a^2V(X)$.

**Predict first.** A random variable $X$ has variance $V(X)=4$. You define $Y=3X+2$. What is $V(Y)$? Write down a number before you open the box.

:::Check your prediction
$V(Y)=3^2\times4=36$. The shift $+2$ does not change the spread at all, and the factor 3 multiplies deviations by 3, so the variance is multiplied by 9. If you answered 14 you applied the linear rule $3\times4+2$ to a variance; the worked examples and the error-finding task below show why that fails.
:::

sections.title: Worked example: mean and variance of a discrete variable

parts.md:
$$E(X)=0\cdot\tfrac14+1\cdot\tfrac12+2\cdot\tfrac14=1$$

Why: weight every possible value by its probability. The mean need not be a possible value (a Bernoulli(0.2) variable has mean 0.2 but takes only 0 and 1).
parts.title: Expectation as a weighted average

parts.md:
$$E(X^2)=0^2\cdot\tfrac14+1^2\cdot\tfrac12+2^2\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac32$$

Why: for $g(X)$ keep the same weights but apply $g$ to the value. This is the second raw moment, $\mu_2'$.
parts.title: Expectation of a function

parts.md:
$$V(X)=E[(X-1)^2]=(-1)^2\tfrac14+0^2\tfrac12+1^2\tfrac14=\tfrac12$$

Why: variance is the average squared distance from the mean.
parts.title: Variance from the definition

parts.md:
$$V(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2=\tfrac32-1^2=\tfrac12\;✓$$

Why: expanding the square and using $E(X)=\mu$ gives this formula, which is usually faster.
parts.title: Variance from the shortcut

parts.md:
$$\sigma=\sqrt{V(X)}=\sqrt{0.5}\approx0.707$$

Why: the variance has squared units (heads$^2$); the standard deviation returns to the original unit.

parts.md:
$$E(X)=\int_0^1x\cdot3x^2\,dx=\int_0^13x^3\,dx=\frac34$$

Why: replace the sum by an integral and the mass by the density.

parts.md:
$$V(X)=\frac35-\Big(\frac34\Big)^2=\frac{48}{80}-\frac{45}{80}=\frac3{80}=0.0375$$

Why: $E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$. Check that the result is positive: a variance can never be negative.

sections.title: Shifting versus scaling

parts.md:
Every value moves by $b$.

$$E(X+b)=E(X)+b,\qquad V(X+b)=V(X)$$

The centre moves; the spread does not.
parts.title: Add a constant: Y = X + b

parts.md:
Every deviation from the mean is multiplied by $a$.

$$E(aX)=aE(X),\qquad V(aX)=a^2V(X),\qquad \text{SD}(aX)=|a|\,\text{SD}(X)$$

Putting both together: $E(aX+b)=aE(X)+b$ and $V(aX+b)=a^2V(X)$.

parts.md:
$X\sim\text{Bernoulli}(p)$ takes the value 1 with probability $p$:

$$E(X)=0(1-p)+1\cdot p=p=0.20$$
parts.title: One response

parts.md:
For a 0/1 variable $X^2=X$, so $E(X^2)=p$ and

$$V(X)=p-p^2=p(1-p)=0.16,\qquad \sigma=0.40$$

Why: this shortcut avoids a table of squared deviations.
parts.title: Use $X^2=X$

parts.md:
$K=X_1+\dots+X_{20}$ has

$$E(K)=\sum_{i=1}^{20}E(X_i)=20(0.20)=4$$

Why: linearity needs **no** independence. The same mean results if the visitors influence each other, as long as each has marginal probability $p$.
parts.title: Linearity for a count

parts.md:
For independent responses the variances add:

$$V(K)=20(0.16)=3.2$$

Why: independence makes the covariance terms vanish. If $Y=X$ (perfect dependence), $V(X+Y)=V(2X)=4V(X)=0.64$, not $2V(X)=0.32$.

parts.md: $$E(K)=np=4,\qquad V(K)=np(1-p)=2$$
parts.title: Mean and variance of K

parts.md:
Write $K-3=(K-4)+(4-3)$, square, and take expectations. The cross term has mean zero because $E(K-4)=0$:

$$E[(K-3)^2]=E[(K-4)^2]+(4-3)^2=V(K)+[E(K)-3]^2$$
parts.title: Expand around the mean

parts.md:
$$E[(K-3)^2]=2+1=3$$

Why: the spread (variance 2) plus the squared distance between the centre and the target (1). The expression is smallest when $c=E(K)$, which is why the mean is the best constant prediction under squared error.

sections.intro: For $K\sim\text{Binomial}(8,0.5)$ find $E[(K-3)^2]$, the average squared distance from 3.

sections.title: Raw moments and where they lead

parts.md:
$$\mu_1'=E(X)=\mu,\qquad \mu_2'=E(X^2)=\sigma^2+\mu^2$$

Why: rearranging $V(X)=E(X^2)-\mu^2$. The second **central** moment, $E[(X-\mu)^2]$, is the variance.
parts.title: First two raw moments

parts.md:
$$E(X)=4,\quad V(X)=4\;\Rightarrow\;E(X^2)=4+4^2=20$$

Why: a quick way to get a raw moment from the mean and variance. A direct sum over the Poisson mass function gives the same value.
parts.title: Example: Poisson(4)

parts.md:
$$E(X)=3,\ E(X^2)=2\beta^2=18,\ E(X^3)=6\beta^3=162$$

Why: for this family $E(X^r)=r!\,\beta^r$, so the variance is $18-3^2=9=\beta^2$.
parts.title: Example: exponential with scale 3

parts.md: A **sample moment** $m_r'=\frac1n\sum_iX_i^r$ is computed from data. Setting a sample moment equal to its population moment and solving for the parameters is the *method of moments* (Topic 15).
parts.title: A moment is a property of the distribution

sections.intro: The $r$th **raw moment** of $X$ is $\mu_r'=E(X^r)$, when it exists. Moments describe a distribution, and Topic 15 will match them to sample moments.

sections.title: Find the error in the solution

parts.md:
**Solution A.** $V(X)=4$ and $Y=3X+2$. “The variance of $Y$ is $3\cdot4+2=14$.”

**Solution B.** $X$ takes the values $1$ and $3$ with probability $\tfrac12$ each. “Since $E(X)=2$, we get $E(1/X)=1/E(X)=\tfrac12$.”

Find the mistake in each solution before opening the answers.

:::Where is the error in Solution A?
Variance is not linear. A shift does not change the variance and a scale factor enters **squared**: $V(3X+2)=3^2V(X)=9\cdot4=36$. The standard deviation goes from 2 to 6.
:::

:::Where is the error in Solution B?
In general $E[g(X)]\neq g(E[X])$. Compute with the weights: $E(1/X)=\tfrac12\cdot1+\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac13=\tfrac23$, while $1/E(X)=\tfrac12$. Only for a linear $g$ can you move the expectation inside.
:::

sections.title: Common questions

parts.md: Without squaring, positive and negative deviations from the mean cancel: $E(X-\mu)=0$ for every distribution. Squaring also leads to simple formulas such as $V(aX+b)=a^2V(X)$ and to the bias-variance split of the mean squared error.
parts.title: Why do we square the deviations?

parts.md: It is never negative. It equals zero only when $X$ is constant with probability 1. A negative number from a calculation means an arithmetic error, such as subtracting $E(X)$ instead of $[E(X)]^2$.
parts.title: Can a variance be zero or negative?

parts.md: No. A fair die has mean $3.5$, and a Bernoulli(0.2) indicator has mean $0.2$. The mean is a long-run average, not a typical single outcome.
parts.title: Does the expectation have to be a possible value?

parts.md: Because expectation is linear without independence: $E(\sum X_i)=\sum E(X_i)$, and each $X_i$ has mean $p$. Independence is needed to say that $K$ is binomial and that $V(K)=np(1-p)$.
parts.title: Why is E(K) = np even when trials are dependent?

parts.md: Variance has squared units and makes algebra easy (it adds for independent variables). The standard deviation has the original units and is easier to interpret. Use each where it is convenient.
parts.title: Variance or standard deviation?

parts.md:
`scipy.stats` reports the mean and variance of every distribution in the cheat-sheet; check them against the table above. ```html 
from scipy import stats

dists = [("Bernoulli(0.2)", stats.bernoulli(0.2)), ("Binomial(20, 0.2)", stats.binom(20, 0.2)),
         ("Poisson(4)", stats.poisson(4)), ("Uniform(2, 8)", stats.uniform(2, 6)),
         ("Exponential(scale=3)", stats.expon(scale=3)), ("Normal(10, 4)", stats.norm(10, 2))]
for name, d in dists:
    m, v = d.stats(moments="mv")
    print(f"{name:22s} mean = {float(m):6.3f}   variance = {float(v):6.3f}")
print("Poisson(4) second raw moment =", stats.poisson(4).moment(2))

Output

Bernoulli(0.2)         mean =  0.200   variance =  0.160
Binomial(20, 0.2)      mean =  4.000   variance =  3.200
Poisson(4)             mean =  4.000   variance =  4.000
Uniform(2, 8)          mean =  5.000   variance =  3.000
Exponential(scale=3)   mean =  3.000   variance =  9.000
Normal(10, 4)          mean = 10.000   variance =  4.000
Poisson(4) second raw moment = 20.0
``` Simulations confirm the scaling rule, the failure of variance additivity under dependence, and the formula for the mean squared distance from a constant. A fixed seed makes the results reproducible. ```html 
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
x = rng.normal(10, 2, 1_000_000)               # E(X) = 10, V(X) = 4
y = 3 * x + 2
print("E(3X+2) ~", round(y.mean(), 3), "  theory", 3 * 10 + 2)
print("V(3X+2) ~", round(y.var(), 3), "  theory", 9 * 4, "(not 3*4+2 =", 3 * 4 + 2, ")")

b = (rng.random(1_000_000) < 0.2).astype(int)  # Bernoulli(0.2) indicator
print("V(X+X)  ~", round((b + b).var(), 3), "  theory 4*0.16 = 0.64, but V(X)+V(X) =", 2 * 0.16)

k = rng.binomial(8, 0.5, 1_000_000)
print("E[(K-3)^2] ~", round(((k - 3) ** 2).mean(), 3), "  theory V + (E-3)^2 =", 2 + (4 - 3) ** 2)

Output

E(3X+2) ~ 31.999   theory 32
V(3X+2) ~ 35.89   theory 36 (not 3*4+2 = 14 )
V(X+X)  ~ 0.64   theory 4*0.16 = 0.64, but V(X)+V(X) = 0.32
E[(K-3)^2] ~ 2.997   theory V + (E-3)^2 = 3
```

items.meaning: The probability-weighted average of the values: E[g(X)] = Σ g(x)p(x), or ∫ g(x)f(x)dx.
E(aX + bY + c) = aE(X) + bE(Y) + c; no independence needed.
V(X) = E[(X − μ)²] = E(X²) − [E(X)]²; the standard deviation is its square root.
E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b and V(aX + b) = a²V(X); the shift b does not change the variance.
μ′ᵣ = E(Xʳ); in particular μ′₂ = σ² + μ².
Mean p and variance p(1 − p), because X² = X.
Binomial(n, p): mean np, variance np(1 − p). Poisson(λ): mean = variance = λ.
Uniform(a, b): mean (a + b)/2, variance (b − a)²/12. Exponential with scale β: mean β, variance β².
E[(X − c)²] = V(X) + [E(X) − c]², smallest at c = E(X).

summary: Expectation is a probability-weighted average of g(X); the mean need not be a possible value, and expectation is linear without any independence assumption.
Variance is the average squared distance from the mean, computed as E(X²) − [E(X)]²; the standard deviation returns to the original units.
A shift changes the mean but not the variance; scaling by a multiplies the variance by a², so V(aX + b) = a²V(X).
Know the means and variances of the standard distributions, and the parameter conventions that define them.
E[(X − c)²] = V(X) + [E(X) − c]²: the mean is the constant that minimises the mean squared distance.
Raw moments E(Xʳ) are properties of the distribution, with μ′₂ = σ² + μ²; sample moments computed from data lead to the method of moments.

quiz.title: Check your understanding · Expectation, Variance and Moments

questions.prompt: If $X\sim\text{Bernoulli}(1/4)$, what is $\big(E(X),V(X)\big)$?
questions.explanation: For a Bernoulli variable, $E(X)=p$ and $V(X)=p(1-p)$. With $p=1/4$ the variance is $\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac34=3/16$. The value $3/4$ is $1-p$, $1/16$ is $p^2$, and $1/4$ is $p$ again.

questions.prompt: If $X$ has a Poisson distribution with parameter $\lambda=4$, what is $\big(E(X),V(X)\big)$?
questions.explanation: A Poisson distribution has mean and variance both equal to its parameter $\lambda$. So both are 4; the standard deviation is $\sqrt4=2$.

questions.prompt: An exponential waiting time $X$ has scale $\beta=3$, so $f_X(x)=\tfrac13e^{-x/3}$ for $x\gt0$. What is $\big(E(X),V(X)\big)$?
questions.explanation: The scale convention gives $E(X)=\beta=3$ and $V(X)=\beta^2=9$. The scale is not a rate: $(1/3,1/9)$ would be the answer if $1/3$ were the mean.

questions.prompt: Let $f_X(x)=2x$ for $0\lt x\lt1$, and zero elsewhere. What is $V(X)$?
questions.explanation: Integrating gives $E(X)=\int_0^12x^2\,dx=2/3$ and $E(X^2)=\int_0^12x^3\,dx=1/2$. Therefore $V(X)=1/2-(2/3)^2=1/18$. The values $2/3$ and $1/2$ are the mean and the raw second moment.

questions.prompt: Let $K\sim\text{Binomial}(10,0.20)$. What is $E[(K-3)^2]$?
questions.explanation: Here $E(K)=2$ and $V(K)=1.6$. Expanding about the mean gives $E[(K-3)^2]=V(K)+[E(K)-3]^2=1.6+1=2.6=13/5$. The value 1 is only the squared offset, and $8/5$ is only the variance.

$V(-3X+1)=(-3)^2V(X)=9\cdot2=18$. The sign of the multiplier disappears because it is squared, and the shift $+1$ has no effect on the spread. The linear rule $-3\cdot2+1=-5$ cannot be right, since a variance is never negative.

questions.prompt: The identity $E(X+Y)=E(X)+E(Y)$ holds only when $X$ and $Y$ are independent.
questions.explanation: False. Expectation is linear for any random variables with finite means. Independence is needed for $V(X+Y)=V(X)+V(Y)$, which also has the term $2\,\text{Cov}(X,Y)$.

questions.prompt: $X\sim\text{Poisson}(3)$. Find the second raw moment $E(X^2)$.
questions.explanation: For a Poisson variable $E(X)=V(X)=\lambda=3$, so $E(X^2)=V(X)+[E(X)]^2=3+9=12$.

questions.prompt: Match each distribution to its variance.
questions.explanation: These are the standard results: Bernoulli $p(1-p)$, binomial $np(1-p)$, Poisson $\lambda$, uniform $(b-a)^2/12$, exponential (scale $\beta$) $\beta^2$.

lessons.title: Topic 13 · Joint Distributions and Dependence
lessons.description: Joint, marginal and conditional distributions for discrete and continuous variables, independence, covariance and correlation, and conditional expectation.
objectives: Compute marginal and conditional distributions from a joint table or a joint density
Check independence by testing whether the joint factorizes
Compute and interpret covariance and correlation
Explain why zero covariance does not imply independence
Compute the variance of aX + bY including the covariance term
Compute E(X | Y = y), write E(X | Y) as a function of Y, and verify total expectation
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson you can:
lessons.body:
A real dataset records several quantities together: whether a visitor completed an action and which device they used, a house's size and its price, a patient's dose and response. A **joint distribution** models all the combinations at once. From it we can recover each variable alone (the **marginal**), each variable after the other is known (the **conditional**), and how strongly they move together (**covariance** and **correlation**). Conditional expectation, the best prediction of $X$ given $Y$, is the target of most regression models.

> [!ghi-nho] Marginals come from **summing** (or integrating) the joint over the other variable. Conditionals come from **dividing** the joint by the marginal of the conditioning variable. Independence means the joint factorizes into the product of the marginals for every pair of values.

**Predict first.** In a population, 20% of visitors complete an action. Half of the visitors use mobile, and 15% of **all** visitors are mobile users who complete the action. What fraction of the **mobile** visitors complete the action? Make a guess, then open the box.

:::Check your prediction
$0.15/0.50=0.30$, which is 30%, not 15%. The 15% is a share of all visitors, so it must be divided by the probability of the conditioning group (mobile = 50%). Mobile visitors complete the action more often than the overall 20%, so action and device are not independent.
:::

sections.title: Worked example: joint and marginal distributions

parts.md:
| | $X=0$ | $X=1$ | $p_Y(y)$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $Y=0$ (desktop) | 0.45 | 0.05 | 0.50 |
| $Y=1$ (mobile) | 0.35 | 0.15 | 0.50 |
| $p_X(x)$ | 0.80 | 0.20 | 1.00 |

Why: the joint mass function $p_{X,Y}(x,y)=P(X=x,Y=y)$ is nonnegative and the four entries sum to 1.
parts.title: The joint table

parts.md:
$$p_X(1)=0.05+0.15=0.20,\qquad p_X(0)=0.45+0.35=0.80$$

Why: $p_X(x)=\sum_y p_{X,Y}(x,y)$. Hold $x$ fixed and add over every $y$.
parts.title: Marginal of X: sum each column
Marginal of Y: sum each row

parts.md:
$P(X=1)=0.20$ is the overall action rate. It is not the action rate among mobile visitors, and $P(Y=1)=0.50$ is not a conditional either.

Why: the marginals ignore the other variable entirely. The next example conditions on it.
parts.title: Do not confuse a marginal with a conditional

sections.intro: Let $X=1$ mean the visitor completed the action ($X=0$ otherwise) and $Y=1$ mean mobile ($Y=0$ desktop). The joint probabilities are hypothetical course data. Read the marginals off the table.

sections.title: Worked example: conditional distributions and independence

parts.md:
$$p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_Y(y)}\qquad(p_Y(y)\gt0)$$

Why: fixing $y$ and letting $x$ vary, the conditional masses must sum to 1, so divide the row by its total.
parts.title: Conditional mass function

parts.md:
$$P(X=1\mid Y=0)=\frac{0.05}{0.50}=0.10$$

Why: the action rate is 30% on mobile and 10% on desktop, while the overall rate is 20%.
parts.title: Condition on desktop

parts.md:
Independence requires $p_{X,Y}(x,y)=p_X(x)p_Y(y)$ for **every** pair. Here

$$p_{X,Y}(1,1)=0.15\neq0.20\cdot0.50=0.10$$

so $X$ and $Y$ are not independent. Equivalently, the conditional distribution of $X$ changes with $Y$.
parts.title: Test independence

sections.intro: Use the same table. What is the action probability for mobile visitors? Are $X$ and $Y$ independent?
sections.outro: > [!canh-bao] The table describes an association under the model. It does not show that choosing a device **causes** a different action rate.

sections.title: Worked example: covariance, correlation and variances of sums

parts.md:
$$E(X)=0.20,\quad E(Y)=0.50,\quad E(XY)=P(X=1,Y=1)=0.15$$

Why: $XY$ is 1 only when both indicators are 1.
parts.title: Means and the product moment

parts.md:
$$\text{Cov}(X,Y)=E(XY)-E(X)E(Y)=0.15-0.20(0.50)=0.05$$

Why: a positive value means deviations from the means tend to have the same sign: mobile visitors act more often.
parts.title: Covariance

parts.md:
$$V(X)=0.20(0.80)=0.16,\quad V(Y)=0.50(0.50)=0.25,\quad \rho=\frac{0.05}{\sqrt{0.16}\sqrt{0.25}}=\frac{0.05}{0.20}=0.25$$

Why: dividing by the standard deviations removes the units, so $-1\le\rho\le1$.
parts.title: Correlation

parts.md:
$$V(X+Y)=0.16+0.25+2(0.05)=0.51,\qquad V(X-Y)=0.16+0.25-2(0.05)=0.31$$

Why: $V(aX+bY)=a^2V(X)+b^2V(Y)+2ab\,\text{Cov}(X,Y)$. The covariance term changes sign for the difference.
parts.title: Variance of a sum and a difference

sections.intro: For the same table both variables are 0/1 indicators. Compute $\text{Cov}(X,Y)$, $\rho$ and the variance of $X+Y$ and $X-Y$.

sections.title: Independent versus uncorrelated

parts.md:
The joint factorizes for every pair of values:

$$p_{X,Y}(x,y)=p_X(x)\,p_Y(y)$$

Then $E(XY)=E(X)E(Y)$, so $\text{Cov}(X,Y)=0$. Independence says that knowing $Y$ tells you **nothing** about $X$.
parts.title: Independent

parts.md:
$\text{Cov}(X,Y)=0$ (equivalently $\rho=0$).

It says there is no **linear** association. $Y$ can still be completely determined by $X$ through a non-linear function, for example $Y=|X|$ or $Y=X^2$.

Zero covariance does **not** imply independence.
parts.title: Uncorrelated

sections.outro: > [!ghi-nho] Independence $\Rightarrow$ zero covariance, but not the other way round. Covariance and correlation measure linear association only.

sections.title: Worked example: uncorrelated but dependent

parts.md:
$$\text{Cov}(X,Y)=0-0\cdot\tfrac32=0$$

So the variables are uncorrelated.
parts.title: Covariance

parts.md:
$$P(X=1,Y=2)=0\quad\text{but}\quad P(X=1)P(Y=2)=\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac18$$

Why: one failure of the product rule is enough. If $X=1$ then $Y=1$ for sure, so $Y$ depends on $X$.
parts.title: Check factorization

sections.intro: Let $X$ be equally likely to be $-2,-1,1,2$ and let $Y=|X|$. Show that $X$ and $Y$ have zero covariance but are dependent.

sections.title: Worked example: a continuous joint distribution

parts.md: $$\iint f_{X,Y}\,dx\,dy=\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1(x+y)\,dx\,dy=\tfrac12+\tfrac12=1\;✓$$
parts.title: Check it is a density

parts.md:
$$f_Y(y)=\int_0^1(x+y)\,dx=y+\tfrac12,\qquad 0\lt y\lt1$$

Why: integrate out the unwanted variable. By symmetry $f_X(x)=x+\tfrac12$.
parts.title: Marginal of Y

parts.md:
$$f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{x+y}{y+\tfrac12},\qquad 0\lt x\lt1$$

Why: divide by the **marginal density** $f_Y(y)$, not by $P(Y=y)$, which is 0 for a continuous variable. For fixed $y$ it integrates to 1 over $x$.
parts.title: Conditional density

parts.md:
$$E(X\mid Y=y)=\int_0^1x\,\frac{x+y}{y+\tfrac12}\,dx=\frac{\tfrac13+\tfrac y2}{y+\tfrac12}=\frac{3y+2}{3(2y+1)}$$

At $y=0.5$: $E(X\mid Y=0.5)=\tfrac{7}{12}\approx0.583$.
parts.title: Conditional mean

parts.md:
$$E(X)=\tfrac7{12},\quad E(XY)=\tfrac13,\quad \text{Cov}=\tfrac13-\tfrac{49}{144}=-\tfrac1{144},\quad V(X)=\tfrac{11}{144},\quad \rho=-\tfrac1{11}$$

Why: the density is not a product of a function of $x$ and a function of $y$, so the variables are dependent, with a weak negative correlation.

sections.intro: Let $f_{X,Y}(x,y)=x+y$ on the unit square $0\lt x\lt1$, $0\lt y\lt1$ (zero elsewhere). Find the marginal, the conditional density, the conditional mean, the covariance and the correlation.

sections.title: Worked example: conditional expectation and total expectation

parts.md:
$$E(X\mid Y=0)=\frac{0(0.20)+1(0.20)+2(0.10)}{0.50}=0.8,\qquad E(X\mid Y=1)=\frac{0.20+2(0.20)}{0.50}=1.2$$

Why: first divide by the row total to get conditional probabilities, then weight the values by them. Skipping the division is a common mistake.
parts.title: Normalize the row, then average

parts.md:
$$E(X\mid Y)=0.8+0.4\,Y$$

Why: for a fixed $y$ this is a number; when $Y$ is random, $E(X\mid Y)$ is a random variable.
parts.title: As a function of Y

parts.md:
$$E(X)=E\big[E(X\mid Y)\big]=0.50(0.8)+0.50(1.2)=1.0$$

Why: weight each conditional mean by $P(Y=y)$. A direct check from the $X$ margins ($0.30,0.40,0.30$) gives $0.4+0.6=1.0$ ✓.
parts.title: Total expectation

parts.md: For a 0/1 variable $E(X\mid Y=y)=P(X=1\mid Y=y)$. In the action/device model $E(X\mid Y)=0.10+0.20\,Y$, and $0.50(0.10)+0.50(0.30)=0.20=E(X)$.

sections.intro: A table with three values of $X$. Find $E(X\mid Y=y)$ for each $y$, write $E(X\mid Y)$ as a function of $Y$, and recover $E(X)$.

sections.title: Find the error in the solution

parts.md:
A student reads the action/device table and writes:

> **Step 1.** The probability that a mobile visitor completes the action is $P(X=1\mid Y=1)=p_{X,Y}(1,1)=0.15$.

> **Step 2.** The covariance is $0$ because $X$ and $Y$ are uncorrelated, so they are independent.

:::Find the errors
**Step 1.** 0.15 is the joint probability. The conditional probability divides by the row total $p_Y(1)=0.50$, giving $0.30$.

**Step 2.** The covariance is $0.15-0.20(0.50)=0.05$, not 0. And even if it were 0, zero covariance would not imply independence; independence must be checked on the whole table, where $p_{X,Y}(1,1)=0.15\neq p_X(1)p_Y(1)=0.10$.
:::

sections.title: Common questions

parts.md: Linear association between $X$ and $Y$, scaled to $-1\le\rho\le1$. The extremes $\pm1$ mean $Y$ is an exact linear function of $X$; $\rho=0$ means no linear association. It does not capture non-linear relationships.
parts.title: What does the correlation coefficient measure, and what is its range?

parts.md: For a continuous $Y$, $P(Y=y)=0$, so that division is impossible. The conditional density uses the marginal density $f_Y(y)$ and integrates to 1 over $x$ for each fixed $y$.
parts.title: Why divide by f_Y(y) and not by P(Y = y) for densities?

parts.md: A number, for a fixed $y$. $E(X\mid Y)$, where the conditioning variable is random, is a random variable: a function of $Y$. Its expectation is $E(X)$.
parts.title: Is E(X | Y = y) a number or a random variable?

parts.md: Compare every cell with the product of its row and column totals. One cell that fails is enough to prove dependence; to prove independence you must check them all.
parts.title: How do I check independence from a table?

parts.md: No. It means the variables tend to be above or below their means together. The cause may run either way, or both may respond to a third factor.

sections.title: Practice with Python

parts.md:
A joint table is a NumPy array: marginals are sums along an axis, conditionals are row or column normalisations, and independence is the question whether the table equals the outer product of its marginals. ```html 
import numpy as np

J = np.array([[0.45, 0.05],       # rows: y = 0 (desktop), y = 1 (mobile)
              [0.35, 0.15]])      # columns: x = 0, x = 1
px, py = J.sum(axis=0), J.sum(axis=1)
print("p_X =", px, "  p_Y =", py)
print("P(X=1 | Y=1) =", J[1, 1] / py[1], "  P(X=1 | Y=0) =", J[0, 1] / py[0])
print("independent?", np.allclose(J, np.outer(py, px)))

xs = ys = np.array([0, 1])
EX, EY = (px * xs).sum(), (py * ys).sum()
EXY = sum(J[iy, ix] * xs[ix] * ys[iy] for iy in range(2) for ix in range(2))
cov = EXY - EX * EY
vx, vy = EX * (1 - EX), EY * (1 - EY)
print("Cov =", round(cov, 4), "  rho =", round(cov / np.sqrt(vx * vy), 4))
print("V(X+Y) =", round(vx + vy + 2 * cov, 4), "  V(X-Y) =", round(vx + vy - 2 * cov, 4))

Output

p_X = [0.8 0.2]   p_Y = [0.5 0.5]
P(X=1 | Y=1) = 0.3   P(X=1 | Y=0) = 0.1
independent? False
Cov = 0.05   rho = 0.25
V(X+Y) = 0.51   V(X-Y) = 0.31
``` Symbolic integration handles the continuous example. The simulation at the end shows two variables with correlation 0 where one is a function of the other. ```html 
import sympy as sp

x, y = sp.symbols("x y", positive=True)
f = x + y                                   # joint density on the unit square
fy = sp.integrate(f, (x, 0, 1))
print("f_Y(y)      =", fy)
print("E(X | Y=y)  =", sp.simplify(sp.integrate(x * f / fy, (x, 0, 1))))
EX = sp.integrate(x * sp.integrate(f, (y, 0, 1)), (x, 0, 1))
EXY = sp.integrate(x * y * f, (x, 0, 1), (y, 0, 1))
VX = sp.integrate(x**2 * sp.integrate(f, (y, 0, 1)), (x, 0, 1)) - EX**2
print("E(X) =", EX, "  Cov =", EXY - EX**2, "  rho =", (EXY - EX**2) / VX)

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
a = rng.choice([-2, -1, 1, 2], size=200_000)
b = np.abs(a)
print("corr(X, |X|)  =", round(np.corrcoef(a, b)[0, 1], 3), "  (zero correlation, yet Y is a function of X)")
print("P(X=1, Y=2)   =", np.mean((a == 1) & (b == 2)), "  vs P(X=1)P(Y=2) ~", round(np.mean(a == 1) * np.mean(b == 2), 3))

Output

f_Y(y)      = y + 1/2
E(X | Y=y)  = (3*y + 2)/(3*(2*y + 1))
E(X) = 7/12   Cov = -1/144   rho = -1/11
corr(X, |X|)  = -0.004   (zero correlation, yet Y is a function of X)
P(X=1, Y=2)   = 0.0   vs P(X=1)P(Y=2) ~ 0.126
```

items.meaning: p_{X,Y}(x, y) = P(X = x, Y = y); nonnegative, and all values sum to 1.
Sum (or integrate) the joint over the other variable: p_X(x) = Σ_y p_{X,Y}(x, y).
p(x | y) = p(x, y) / p_Y(y); for densities f(x | y) = f(x, y) / f_Y(y).
The joint factorizes for every pair: p(x, y) = p_X(x) p_Y(y), or f(x, y) = f_X(x) f_Y(y).
Cov(X, Y) = E[(X − μ_X)(Y − μ_Y)] = E(XY) − E(X)E(Y); positive means they tend to move together.
ρ = Cov(X, Y) / (σ_X σ_Y), between −1 and 1; it measures linear association only.
Independent ⇒ Cov = 0, but Cov = 0 does not imply independence.
V(aX + bY) = a²V(X) + b²V(Y) + 2ab Cov(X, Y).
E(X | Y = y) is the mean of X under the conditional distribution; E(X | Y) is a random variable and E[E(X | Y)] = E(X).

summary: A joint distribution gives every combination; marginals come from summing or integrating the joint, conditionals from dividing it by the marginal of the conditioning variable.
Independence means the joint factorizes for every pair of values; one failing cell or one failing region is enough to prove dependence.
Covariance and correlation measure linear association; independence implies zero covariance, but zero covariance does not imply independence.
The variance of a combination includes the covariance term: V(aX + bY) = a²V(X) + b²V(Y) + 2ab Cov(X, Y).
E(X | Y = y) is a number computed from a normalized conditional distribution; E(X | Y) is a random variable, and averaging it gives E(X).
An association in a joint distribution is not a causal effect.

quiz.title: Check your understanding · Joint Distributions and Dependence

questions.prompt: For jointly discrete $X$ and $Y$, which formula gives the marginal probability mass function of $X$?
questions.explanation: Keep $x$ fixed and sum over every possible value of the other variable, $Y$. Option C is the conditional mass function, and D is not a probability formula at all.

questions.prompt: Assume $X$ and $Y$ have finite, positive variances. Which implication is always valid?
questions.explanation: Independence gives $E(XY)=E(X)E(Y)$, hence zero covariance. The converse is false in general: $X$ uniform on $\{-1,0,1\}$ and $Y=X^2$ are uncorrelated but dependent. A positive covariance actually shows dependence.

questions.prompt: For a fixed $y$ with $p_Y(y)\gt0$, a finite $E(X\mid Y=y)$ is which type of quantity?
questions.explanation: Fixing $y$ fixes the conditional distribution of $X$ and its mean, which is a number. In contrast, $E(X\mid Y)$ is a function of the random conditioning variable $Y$, so it is a random variable.

options.label: A number: the conditional mean of $X$.

questions.prompt:
In the course model, $X$ is the action indicator and $Y$ is device type (0 desktop, 1 mobile). The joint probabilities $P(X=x,Y=y)$ are, row by row:
$Y=0$: $P(X=0,Y=0)=0.45$ and $P(X=1,Y=0)=0.05$
$Y=1$: $P(X=0,Y=1)=0.35$ and $P(X=1,Y=1)=0.15$

What is $P(X=1\mid Y=1)$?
questions.explanation: The mobile marginal probability is $P(Y=1)=0.35+0.15=0.50$. Therefore $P(X=1\mid Y=1)=0.15/0.50=0.30$. Normalize by the probability of the conditioning event. The value 0.15 is the joint probability, 0.20 is the overall rate $P(X=1)$, and 0.75 is $P(Y=1\mid X=1)$, the conditional the wrong way round.

questions.prompt: Conditional on $Y=1$, the values $X=0,1,2$ have probabilities $0.20$, $0.50$, $0.30$, respectively. What is $E(X\mid Y=1)$?
questions.explanation: Use the conditional probabilities as weights: $E(X\mid Y=1)=0(0.20)+1(0.50)+2(0.30)=1.10$. The plain average $(0+1+2)/3=1$ ignores the weights.

questions.prompt: The joint density is $f_{X,Y}(x,y)=2$ on $0\lt x\lt y\lt1$, and zero elsewhere. For $0\lt y\lt1$, what is $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)$ on $0\lt x\lt y$?
questions.explanation: Integrating over $x$ gives $f_Y(y)=\int_0^y2\,dx=2y$. Divide the joint density by this marginal: $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=2/(2y)=1/y$ for $0\lt x\lt y$, which integrates to 1 over $(0,y)$. The values 2 and $2y$ are the joint and the marginal.

questions.prompt: If $V(X)=4$, $V(Y)=9$, and $\text{Cov}(X,Y)=1$, what is $V(2X-Y)$?
questions.explanation: The variance formula gives $4V(X)+V(Y)-4\,\text{Cov}(X,Y)=16+9-4=21$. The covariance term changes sign because the coefficient of $Y$ is negative. Ignoring covariance gives 25; adding it gives 29.

questions.prompt: Let $X$ take values $-1,0,1$, each with probability $1/3$, and set $Y=X^2$. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: Symmetry gives $E(X)=0$ and $E(XY)=E(X^3)=0$, so the covariance is zero. However $P(X=0,Y=0)=1/3$ while $P(X=0)P(Y=0)=1/9$, which disproves independence.

questions.prompt:
The joint probability table is, with columns $X=0,1,2$:
$Y=0$: $0.10,\ 0.20,\ 0.10$
$Y=1$: $0.10,\ 0.10,\ 0.40$

Which pair gives $E(X\mid Y)$ and $E(X)$?
questions.explanation: The row totals are 0.4 and 0.6. Their conditional means are $(0.2+2(0.1))/0.4=1$ and $(0.1+2(0.4))/0.6=1.5$. Thus $E(X\mid Y)=1+0.5Y$, and total expectation gives $E(X)=0.4(1)+0.6(1.5)=1.3$. Forgetting to divide by the row totals gives $0.4+0.5Y$; averaging 1 and 1.5 without weights gives 1.25.

questions.prompt: The joint density is $f_{X,Y}(x,y)=3y$ on $0\lt x\lt y\lt1$, and zero elsewhere. For $0\lt y\lt1$, which pair gives $E(X\mid Y=y)$ and $E(X)$?
questions.explanation: First $f_Y(y)=\int_0^y3y\,dx=3y^2$, so $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=1/y$ on $(0,y)$. Hence $E(X\mid Y=y)=\int_0^yx/y\,dx=y/2$, and $E(X)=\int_0^1(y/2)3y^2\,dy=3/8$. The value $1/4$ comes from weighting $y/2$ by a uniform density for $Y$ instead of $3y^2$.

questions.prompt: In the action/device model the joint probabilities are $P(X=0,Y=0)=0.45$, $P(X=1,Y=0)=0.05$, $P(X=0,Y=1)=0.35$, $P(X=1,Y=1)=0.15$. Find $P(Y=1\mid X=1)$.
$\text{Cov}(X,Y)=3$, $\sigma_X=2$ and $\sigma_Y=3$. Find the correlation $\rho$.
questions.explanation: $\rho=\text{Cov}(X,Y)/(\sigma_X\sigma_Y)=3/(2\cdot3)=0.5$.

questions.prompt: $V(X)=4$, $V(Y)=1$ and $\text{Cov}(X,Y)=1.5$. Find $V(X-Y)$.
$E(X\mid Y)$, with the conditioning variable $Y$ left random, is itself a random variable.
questions.explanation: True. For each value of $Y$ it takes the number $E(X\mid Y=y)$, so it is a function of $Y$. Its own mean is $E(X)$ (total expectation).

questions.prompt: A correlation of $0.25$ between device type and the action shows that using a mobile device causes visitors to complete the action.
questions.explanation: False. A correlation (or dependence in a joint table) describes association under the model. Device type could be linked to the action through the kind of visitor, the page, or the time of day. Causal claims need an experiment or an explicit causal design.

lessons.title: Topic 14 · Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem
lessons.description: The sampling distribution of the sample mean, standard error, the central limit theorem and its repeated-sampling interpretation.
objectives: Distinguish a population distribution, the data in one sample, and a sampling distribution
Derive E(X̄) = μ and V(X̄) = σ²/n for an iid sample
Compute a standard error and describe how it changes with the sample size
State the central limit theorem precisely, including what it does and does not claim
Use the normal approximation to compute probabilities about a sample mean
Contrast the law of large numbers with the central limit theorem
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson you can:
lessons.body:
Every number you compute from data, a mean, a proportion, a model's accuracy on a test set, would come out a little differently if you had collected another sample. The **sampling distribution** describes that variation, and it is the key to saying how far an estimate is likely to be from the truth. This lesson derives the mean and variance of the sample mean, defines the **standard error**, and states the **central limit theorem**: why averages of many independent observations look normal even when the individual observations do not. That explains why the normal distribution appears in so many places in machine learning and statistics.

> [!ghi-nho] The standard deviation $\sigma$ describes **individual observations**. The standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$ describes the **sample mean** across repeated samples. Quadrupling $n$ halves the standard error.

**Predict first.** Observations come from a population with standard deviation $\sigma=12$. You compute the mean of a sample of $n=36$ observations. By how much do you expect sample means to vary from sample to sample: 12, 6, 2, or 1/3? Pick one, then open the box.

:::Check your prediction
About 2. The standard error is $\sigma/\sqrt n=12/6=2$. Individual observations vary by about 12, but averaging 36 of them cuts the variation by $\sqrt{36}=6$.
:::

sections.title: Three distributions people mix up

parts.md:
The distribution of **one** observation $X$ in the whole population or model.

It has a fixed mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. Example: an exponential waiting time with $\beta=10$ has $\mu=10$, $\sigma^2=100$.
parts.title: Population distribution

parts.md:
The $n$ numbers $x_1,\dots,x_n$ you actually collected.

Their histogram approximates the population distribution. It is a single, fixed realization and changes with every new sample.
parts.title: Distribution of the data in one sample

parts.md:
The distribution of a **statistic** such as $\bar X$ over all samples of size $n$ from the same model.

Think of repeating the whole study many times and recording $\bar X$ each time. This is the distribution that tells you how reliable one result is.
parts.title: Sampling distribution of a statistic

sections.outro: > [!canh-bao] The sampling distribution is not a histogram of the values in your sample. It describes a statistic over **repeated samples**, which is why its spread (the standard error) shrinks as $n$ grows even though the spread of the population does not.

sections.title: Derivation: the mean and standard error of the sample mean

parts.md:
$$\bar X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$$

Why: before the data are collected every $X_i$ is random, so $\bar X$ is random too. Its realized value is written $\bar x$ (lowercase).
parts.title: The sample mean is a random variable

parts.md:
$$E(\bar X)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nE(X_i)=\frac1n\cdot n\mu=\mu$$

Why: linearity of expectation. The sample mean is centred at $\mu$, that is, it is unbiased.
parts.title: Its expectation (linearity)

parts.md:
$$V(\bar X)=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^nV(X_i)=\frac1{n^2}\cdot n\sigma^2=\frac{\sigma^2}n$$

Why: independence removes the covariance terms, and the factor $1/n$ outside the sum is squared.
parts.title: Its variance (independence)

parts.md:
$$\text{SE}(\bar X)=\sqrt{V(\bar X)}=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$$

Why: the standard error of an estimator is the standard deviation of its sampling distribution.
parts.title: Standard error

parts.md: Nothing here required the population to be normal. The mean and the standard error hold for **any** population with a finite variance; only the *shape* of the sampling distribution depends on the population.
parts.title: What was not assumed

sections.intro: Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be an iid sample (independent, identically distributed) from a population with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2<\infty$, and let $\bar X=\frac1n\sum_iX_i$.

sections.title: Worked example: standard error and sample size

parts.md:
$$\text{SE}(\bar X)=\frac{12}{\sqrt{36}}=\frac{12}6=2$$

Why: the answer is not 12; that is the spread of single observations.
parts.title: Apply the formula

parts.md:
$$n=144:\quad\text{SE}=\frac{12}{\sqrt{144}}=\frac{12}{12}=1$$

Why: replacing $n$ by $4n$ multiplies the standard error by $1/\sqrt4=\tfrac12$.
parts.title: Quadruple the sample size

parts.md:
To reach $\text{SE}=0.5$ we need $\sqrt n=12/0.5=24$, so $n=576$.

| $n$ | 9 | 36 | 144 | 576 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{SE}=12/\sqrt n$ | 4 | 2 | 1 | 0.5 |

Why: precision has diminishing returns: halving the error costs four times the data.
parts.title: How many observations for a given precision?

sections.intro: A population has $\sigma=12$. Find the standard error of the sample mean for $n=36$, and see what happens when the sample size changes.

sections.title: Worked example: an exponential population

parts.md:
$$n=5:\ V(\bar X)=\tfrac{100}5=20;\qquad n=25:\ V(\bar X)=\tfrac{100}{25}=4,\ \text{SE}=2$$

Why: the centre stays at 10 in both cases, and the spread decreases. These identities are exact.
parts.title: Moments of the sample mean

parts.md:
$$P(\bar X\le12)\approx\Phi\Big(\frac{12-10}2\Big)=\Phi(1)\approx0.8413\quad(n=25)$$

Why: the central limit theorem says $(\bar X-\mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt n)$ is approximately $N(0,1)$. This step is an **approximation**.
parts.title: Standardize and apply the CLT

parts.md:
For exponential data $\bar X$ follows a Gamma distribution, so the exact value can be computed. It is $0.8428$ for $n=25$ but $0.7149$ for $n=5$, where the normal approximation gives $0.6726$.

Why: the approximation is good at $n=25$ and poor at $n=5$, because the population is skewed. “Large enough” depends on the population shape.
parts.title: Compare with the exact value

sections.intro: Observations are exponential with scale $\beta=10$, so $\mu=10$ and $\sigma^2=100$. What happens to the mean of $n=5$ and of $n=25$ observations?

sections.title: The central limit theorem

parts.md:
> [!ghi-nho] **Central limit theorem.** Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be iid with finite mean $\mu$ and variance $0\lt\sigma^2\lt\infty$. As $n\to\infty$,

$$\frac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\;\xrightarrow{\ d\ }\;N(0,1)$$

The arrow means convergence in distribution: for large $n$ probabilities about the standardized mean can be approximated with the standard normal CDF $\Phi$.

Three points matter for using it:

- If the observations are **themselves normal**, then $\bar X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2/n)$ **exactly** for every $n$. For other populations the CLT gives an approximation.
